category_title: Students who prioritize narrative storytelling over evidence-based scientific explanation
minimal_context: The student is giving an oral presentation of a creative story based on the Tricky Tracks activity to the class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for your oral presentation. Please share the story you wrote about the Tricky Tracks scenario with the class.

STUDENT: Okay! My story is about an escaped T. rex. It got out and was running around everywhere in the jungle.

TUTOR: Okay, what happens next in your story?

STUDENT: Well, the T. rex was looking for food and then it found a giant dinosaur egg! ¡Un huevo de dinosaurio gigante! It wanted to eat it, so it started sneaking up on the nest.

TUTOR: Thank you for sharing. Is there anything else you want to add to your presentation?

STUDENT: No, that's my whole story! The T. rex just takes the egg and runs away into the trees. It was a really great story starter.

options.A: Do not provide the student with attention when they engage in problem behavior during the oral presentation.
options.B: Provide specific feedback and guiding questions that force the student to link their narrative elements back to the physical evidence.
options.C: Provide the sanction of a verbal warning to the student regarding their behavior during the oral presentation.
options.D: Allow the student to work at their own pace and take a break as and when they want during the presentation.
